improvements.title: Measure the air at home
improvements.why: About 80 % of your PM2.5 dose is breathed at home, and it is estimated from the outdoor level there. An indoor sensor (PM2.5 and CO2) would replace the estimate.
improvements.evidence: Indoor PM2.5 differs from outdoor by cooking, candles, smoking and filtration; it cannot be inferred reliably from outdoor levels (WHO indoor air quality guidelines).

improvements.title: Run a HEPA air purifier where you spend the most hours
improvements.why: PM2.5 at home averages 16 ug/m3 (outdoor level at home), above the WHO annual guideline of 5. Most of your dose is breathed there.
improvements.evidence: Portable HEPA cleaners lowered indoor PM2.5 substantially in field studies (Cheek et al., Sci Total Environ 2021, review). Size it to the room: clean-air delivery rate about 2/3 of the floor area in ft2.

improvements.title: Ventilate the bedroom at night
improvements.why: Night-time CO2 at home averages 1250 ppm, with 10 nights above 1400 ppm for 2 hours or more.
improvements.evidence: Lower bedroom CO2 (an open window or a fan) improved sleep and next-day performance (Strom-Tejsen et al., Indoor Air 2016). 1,000 ppm is a ventilation convention, not a health limit.

improvements.title: Move hard outdoor sessions to cleaner hours
improvements.why: 4 of your 10 outdoor sessions in the last 30 days were in air above the WHO 24-hour PM2.5 level or the 8-hour ozone level. The forecast is available a few days ahead.
improvements.evidence: Breathing rises several-fold during exercise, so the dose of a polluted hour is higher (Giles & Koehle, Sports Med 2014). Ozone peaks in the afternoon; PM2.5 often in the evening and early morning.

improvements.title: Sun protection, or earlier sessions on high UV days
improvements.why: 10 outdoor sessions were at a UV index of 6 or more.
improvements.evidence: WHO: protection is needed from UV index 3, and extra protection from 6 (high).
